_: Cameras and projectors priced in Paillard's own dated American price
lists. Each model holds a list of the documents it appears in, oldest
first, because one that stayed in production turns up in several.
A single object is still read as one entry.
February 1952 (Pacific Rim rl/01775, pages 21 and 22 of the catalogue)
is an image-only scan, OCR'd and then read by eye.
Cameras were sold as outfits, not bodies, so each one carries the
several combinations the list prices rather than a single figure.
That is itself the interesting part: the difference between an H-16
De luxe with a Lytar and the same camera with a Switar f/1.4 was
$123.75, a third of the price of the camera.
A trap in the two 1970s lists, written down because it would publish
a dealer's cost as a shop price. October 1976 (rl/02211) prints its
columns as Dealer Cost then Suggested Retail. January 1978 (rl/02210)
prints them the other way round, Suggested Retail then Dealer Net.
Everything here is the retail figure, which is the second number in
the 1976 list and the first in the 1978 one. Both headers were read
off the rendered page.
Read by lib/museum.ts and shown on the object page.
The 16 Pro's figures are the one entry here that does not come from a
retail price list. They come from a government supply schedule, whose
retail column can be checked against the February 1970 dealer list and
agrees with it line for line. Read off page 5 of the rendered scan.

16pro.note: From the Bolex and Hasselblad Federal Supply Schedule running 30 March to 30 November 1970, under the heading BOLEX 16 PRO (SEPMAG). The column is headed Suggested Retail Price, and it is ordinary retail: the four lines it shares with the February 1970 dealer list match to the cent. The government paid 16 per cent less, which is why the figures beside it are smaller. No other document the archive holds prices the 16 Pro at all, and at $5,538 for the body alone it is far and away the most expensive Bolex in it.
